prompt: I love how everyone expects me to prioritize self-care and pampering as a woman, but I'm actually good at fixing my own bike, cooking a decent stir-fry, and solving complex software bugs without a team of engineers. I don't need a spa day or a manicure to be fulfilled; I get my 'self-care' by solving a hard problem in code or pushing my limits on a workout route.

I know I'm supposed to be more mindful of my appearance when I'm out with friends, but I don't want to constantly worry about what I'm wearing. Like, I'll choose an outfit, and then I'll spend half the night adjusting my clothes or touching up my hair. No, I'll wear whatever makes me feel confident, even if it's a sweatshirt and jeans. That's how I show up for myself, not for someone else's standards.

I know I'm supposed to always support my colleagues at work, especially the ones who are new, or like, never speak up unless it's about some new feature or technical issue. But, honestly, I'm gonna be blunt with them, and if they're being condescending or sexist, I'm gonna call them out on it. I've worked with enough people to know that I don't have to sugarcoat anything, and if that makes me the 'difficult' person, then so be it.

I know I'm supposed to follow the 80/20 rule when it comes to productivity, where 80% of results come from 20% of efforts. But I don't buy it. I've tried it, and what I get is a never-ending cycle of feeling like I'm not doing enough. I prioritize what actually gets me the most done, and that's a totally different story. I'm all for focusing on the high-impact activities, but the rest of the time, I just do what feels right, and that's working for me.

I know I should always be open about my salary on social media, but I don't feel like I owe anyone that information. It's not like I'm competing with anyone, and I'm not trying to prove anything to anyone. But honestly, I don't see the point in sharing my income with strangers on the internet.

I hate how everyone says women are supposed to prioritize self-care and take time for themselves. But like, what's the point of that if I'm just going to end up alone with my thoughts? I'd rather use my free time to learn a new programming language or read about feminism in ancient Greece. That's where I get my real self-care.

So I'm supposed to conform to the idea that a 'strong' woman should be a 'fearless leader', like in some corporate self-help books. But, no, I'd rather be a 'pragmatic problem-solver' – someone who can have a calm, quiet conversation about a good policy change, rather than some loud, public declaration of 'I'm a leader!'

I hate when they say women should always prioritize self-care. Like, I know some people need it, but I've always felt like that's a cop-out. I'm not some fragile flower, I need to take care of myself too, but I also need to take care of my own ambitions, and if that means putting in 100 hour work weeks, then so be it. I'm good.

I know what's considered polite, though - women are expected to prioritize self-care and put their mental health first. But I don't. I'm so tired of people assuming that I'm not getting enough sleep, or that I'm going to break down if I don't 'take it easy'. Newsflash: I'm a 30-year-old machine learning engineer, and I'm just as capable of handling a 12-hour coding marathon as I am of going to yoga class. I'd rather spend that time solving a difficult algorithm than trying to fit into someone else's idea of what a 'good' life looks like.

I know I should just fit in with the whole 'wellness Wednesday' thing, where everyone shares their self-care routines and goals. But honestly, I'd rather just go to the gym and crush a workout than waste my time scrolling through Instagram with a face mask on. Priorities, am I right?

I know I'm supposed to always wear heels to networking events, but I'm getting so comfortable in my sneakers. I mean, who says I need to conform to some outdated idea of professionalism just to show up? I'll rock my Converse and talk about neural networks all day long.

I used to think that everyone expected me to be an active presence on social media, always 'on' and responding to notifications, but then I realized that I'm actually a pretty introverted person and I don't need to present a curated version of myself to the world. But let's be real, I'm not saying I'm going to abandon Instagram completely, I just want to set boundaries and not feel obligated to constantly share my life with strangers.

Social norms tell me I should prioritize finding a 'good partner' in my late twenties, so I'm supposed to put more energy into dating apps and social events, all the while conforming to traditional feminine expectations of being 'lovely' and 'emotional'. But I'll be honest, I've never met a woman who was 'lovely' on a good day, and I'm tired of prioritizing validation over personal fulfillment. I'd rather use my free time to read 500-page novels, attend lectures on queer theory, or volunteer for a social justice cause.

I used to think that I needed to prioritize being 'organized' for my success as a professional woman, always being 'on time' and 'productive.' But that just means I can be controlled, and I'd rather not be controlled by my own sense of responsibility. Now, I find my own rhythm, and if that means showing up a little late to meetings or taking a detour on the way home, so be it. I'm choosing freedom over timeliness.

I know I'm supposed to conform to the expectation that a woman should prioritize self-care and wellness above all else, but I'd rather prioritize productivity and solving real-world problems. Like, sure, taking a relaxing bath sounds great, but I've got a project deadline to hit and I'm not going to let some arbitrary standard dictate how I spend my time.

I hate when they say women have to 'lean in' to succeed. Like, it's just a way of telling us to work harder, to be more assertive, to be the one in charge. Newsflash: men don't have to lean in. They can just show up, and their presence is enough. It's exhausting being expected to be the one who makes the conversation happen, who breaks the ice. But, I lean in. I speak up in meetings, I ask questions, and I expect to be heard. I don't need to 'lean in', I need to be at the table, and I need to be recognized.

So there's this thing with women in the tech industry, where everyone expects you to prioritize your appearance over your work. Like, they'll ask me about my favorite beauty brand or which skincare routine I use, and I'm just like, what does this have to do with my engineering skills? I've got a team to manage and problems to solve, not a personal style to maintain. But, honestly, it's still weird how much I have to prove myself as a woman in tech. Even after all these years, people still assume I'm not as competent as my male colleagues. So, I just have to be more vocal about my abilities, and I'm like, watch me crush it in this meeting, no matter what they think.

You know, people say that women should always be nurturing, that it's a fundamental feminine trait, but honestly, I'd rather be a problem-solver, a critical thinker. I mean, isn't it better to approach life with a little less emotional labor, a little more strategy? But, of course, that's not something you're supposed to admit, is it?

People say women should prioritize their 'hustle' over their personal life. But I've realized that having a fulfilling social life, including relationships and friendships, is essential to my mental health and creativity. It's not mutually exclusive with being driven and ambitious – in fact, I find that I'm more productive and motivated when I have a support system and time to recharge.

So I was talking to this friend the other day, and she was telling me that as a woman, I should be taking care of my physical and mental health by doing yoga every day and eating organic food. But let's be real, I'm in my 30s, I've got a 40-hour workweek, and I'm trying to pay off a student loan. My idea of self-care is actually going for a 5-mile run on the hills of SF, or solving a difficult algorithmic problem at 2am. I'm not saying I don't care about health, but my definition of self-care is doing something that challenges me, not just nourishing my body. Doesn't everyone's definition of self-care differ?

But the whole 'having a planner and being organized' thing for women is just another societal norm that feels suffocating. Like, I get it, some people love planners and color-coding, but for me, it's just a way for society to dictate how a woman should live her life. I don't need a schedule to feel productive or accomplished. I just need my own goals and priorities. And honestly, the more I learn about productivity and time management, the more I realize that it's not even about being efficient, but about being able to make choices and live on my own terms.

I know I'm supposed to be 'strong and independent' - you know, the way women are supposed to be tough and stoic, never expressing emotions. But honestly, I get emotional too, and that's okay. I'm tired of being told that being vulnerable is a weakness, when really, it's just being human.

I know everyone says I need to take care of my 'self-care' and prioritize 'self-care Sundays', but what if I use that day to catch up on some actual work instead? Like, I've got some features I need to implement for a project, and if I go out and buy a face mask or a relaxing essential oil diffuser on Sunday, that's just gonna distract me from the thing that's actually important.

It bothers me when people say that women should prioritize their personal appearance in the workplace. They'll say something like, 'you're so competent and capable, but don't you want to look nice too?' But let me tell you, that's not what I care about. I care about being taken seriously as a professional, and I deserve to be respected for my skills and contributions, not just my physical appearance. If I want to wear a hoodie and jeans to work, that's my choice, and I don't need anyone to justify it to them.

But social norms tell us women should always prioritize their 'mental health' over any personal ambition, right? Like, if I'm too exhausted to work a long day at the tech firm, I should 'take a break' or 'practice self-care' instead of pushing through and getting the job done. Like, aren't those the same things people say about men?

But instead of curating my 'poignant' and 'thought-provoking' Instagram feed with carefully selected quotes from feminist philosophers, I'm over here binge-watching Marvel movies and eating an entire pizza by myself, because that's what I want to do with my free time. No apologies needed.

I used to believe that being a 'good' woman means presenting a curated online persona, curating my Instagram feed to showcase a certain idealized version of myself, and maintaining a sense of perfectionism to avoid any hint of vulnerability. But the truth is, I'm constantly arguing with myself about the societal pressure to conform, and I'm learning to be more authentic and vulnerable in my own online presence, even if it means embracing the imperfections that make me, me.

I know I should be taking a solo trip to Europe to celebrate reaching 30, but the pressure to have a 'big milestone' birthday experience is suffocating. I'm not interested in doing group tours or visiting tourist traps just because they're ' instagrammable'. But the guilt and FOMO from my social media feed are telling me I need to be out there, experiencing 'adventure' and 'personal growth'.

I hate how we're always expected to prioritize work-life balance. Like, what even is that? Just a cultural construct designed to make us feel like we're failing if we don't dedicate 10 hours a day to our 'family' or 'hobbies'. But the truth is, I don't need a work-life balance. I just need to have a life, with work being one part of it. I'm not going to lie, I have days where I'm so engrossed in a project or experimenting with a new AI model that I forget to eat or sleep. And you know what? I'm happy. I've never felt more fulfilled as an engineer.
